description: Launch your cosmic adventure with the NASA Space Apps Challenge! Built for future explorers, this challenge lets you step into the boots of a junior astronaut to tackle real-world space puzzles.
summary: ARES KIDS: Survival on Sol-7 is a browser-based, interactive STEM decision-simulation game designed for students ages 7–12 to experience the real engineering trade-offs of running a Martian or Lunar outpost. Traditional space education either oversimplifies survival into abstract facts or overwhelms young learners with complex spreadsheets. Our solution bridges this gap by combining cartoon dilemma cards with real-time and archived NASA telemetry. Players step into the boots of Junior Commander Maya at Jezero Crater for a 7-Sol mission, balancing three interdependent core systems: Power (⚡), Life Support & Food (🌱), and Radiation Shielding (🛡️). Every decision carries a compound resource cost—such as diverting battery power to magnetic shields during a live NASA DONKI solar flare or sacrificing drinking water to shield the habitat walls. Grounded in NASA DONKI, OSDR, RadLab, and Mars Trek data, players learn firsthand how real mission planners navigate deep-space survival.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?ARES KIDS: Survival on Sol-7 is an interactive web-based survival and resource-management game built for kids ages 7–12. Players manage a deep-space habitat at Jezero Crater on Mars (or an Artemis Lunar outpost) across 7 Sols (Martian days) while waiting for a supply lander.

  • No Free Choices (True Engineering Trade-Offs): Each Sol presents a high-stakes mission dilemma inspired by real spaceflight challenges—such as regional dust storms coating solar arrays, M-Class solar flares, 40-minute round-trip Earth-Mars communication blackouts, and hydroponic crop stress.
  • Visual Consequence Engine: Before clicking Choice A or Choice B, hovering over a card reveals pulsing impact indicators on the three core meters (Power ⚡, Life Support & Food 🌱, and Radiation Shielding 🛡️), demonstrating that saving one resource always costs another.
  • Dynamic Habitat Stage: The central cartoon habitat dynamically reacts to player choices—lights flicker and frost particles appear when power drops below 35%, hydroponic radish plants wilt when life support drops, and red plasma waves trigger when a solar flare strikes.
  • In-Context Plain-Language Science Pop-Ups: After every decision, a kid-friendly "Science Fact Card" explains complex terminology (Sol, Coronal Mass Ejection, Millisieverts (mSv), Hydroponics, Perchlorates) in one clear sentence.
  • Live NASA Telemetry & Verification Drawer: Players, teachers, and judges can click the "📡 Live NASA Telemetry & Mars Map" modal at any time to inspect real-time solar flare data fetched via the NASA DONKI API, compare Mars vs. Earth radiation levels via NASA RadLab data, and explore the exact outpost landing coordinates on NASA Mars Trek.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Bridging the Translation Gap: Transforms abstract aerospace constraints into intuitive visual cause-and-effect mechanics that a 7-year-old can grasp immediately while remaining scientifically accurate for classroom use.
  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Runs instantly in any web browser with zero downloads, logins, or installations required, plus a built-in verified NASA dataset fallback so classrooms with restricted internet never hit a broken screen.
  • Replayability & Growth Mindset: Scenarios draw from a randomized pool of real mission events, encouraging kids to test new resource strategies and view mission failures as learning opportunities.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Frontend & Architecture: React, Vite, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, Tailwind CSS
  • Animations & Visuals: Framer Motion (interactive card physics and habitat state transitions), Lucide React (UI iconography), Canvas Confetti
  • Audio Engine: Custom zero-dependency HTML5 Web Audio API synthesizer for interactive arcade sound effects
  • APIs & Data Integration: RESTful integration with NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov, DONKI Space Weather API, APOD) and embedded scientific metadata from NASA OSDR, NASA RadLab, and CSA Food Production toolkits
  • Development Environment: VS Code, Node.js, Git/GitHub, and AI-assisted development via Google Antigravity and Gemini for code scaffolding and prompt engineering

Creativity & Factors Considered We intentionally limited resource tracking to three core pillars (Power, Life Support/Food, Shielding) so young learners aren't overwhelmed by complex dashboards, while designing every scenario around authentic compound costs. We also included a Web Audio API sound synthesizer and SI-usage transparency metadata in the footer/credits to ensure full compliance with NASA guidelines.
